problem: The sentence says lipaemia, haemolysis and a cuvette scratch 'add roughly the same absorbance at both wavelengths'. That is not true of haemolysis. Free haemoglobin absorbs strongly near 400–430 nm and much less at 600 nm, so its added absorbance at a main wavelength like 505 nm and a reference like 600 nm is very different and is not cancelled by the subtraction. Only turbidity (lipaemia) and cuvette/blank differences behave roughly the same at both wavelengths.
fix: Bichromatic measurement reads the cuvette at the main wavelength and again at a reference wavelength, then subtracts. Turbidity such as lipaemia, and a scratched or dirty cuvette, add nearly the same absorbance at both wavelengths, so the subtraction removes most of that. Haemolysis is not cancelled this way, because haemoglobin absorbs differently at the two wavelengths; modern analysers measure a haemolysis index and flag the sample instead.

problem: The formula uses A(sample) and A(std) as if they were the raw readings, but a single-point ratio is only valid when both absorbances have had the reagent blank subtracted. A student who plugs in raw readings gets a biased concentration.
fix: State that A(sample) and A(std) are net absorbances, that is, the reading with the reagent blank (and cuvette blank) subtracted: c(sample) = c(std) × (A(sample) ÷ A(std)), where A = A(measured) − A(blank).

problem: The text says sensing is 'capacitive or resistive' but then explains only the capacitive case (probe tip as one plate of a capacitor). The resistive case is left unexplained, so the two ideas get mixed.
fix: Capacitive sensing: the probe tip is one plate of a capacitor and the capacitance changes when the tip touches serum. Resistive sensing: the probe and the grounded tube form a circuit whose conductance changes when the tip enters the conducting serum. Either change stops the downward drive.

problem: The order of the optical parts is muddled. The text says the filter wheel selects the wavelength and then the photodiode reads light through the cuvette, and the figure labels the detector block 'filter wheel'. In a filter photometer the light passes the filter before the cuvette; the photodetector sits after the cuvette.
fix: Write: light from the lamp passes through the filter wheel, which selects the wavelength, then through the cuvette, and a photodiode after the cuvette measures the transmitted light. Label the detector block 'Photodiode' and keep the filter wheel as a separate idea in the text.

problem: '600 tests per hour means 6 s per test' can be read as the time one test takes from pipetting to result. In a random-access analyser many cuvettes are processed in parallel and incubation takes minutes, so 6 s is only the average interval at which results come out.
fix: Say: 600 tests per hour means one result every 3600 s ÷ 600 = 6 s on average; this is the cycle time, not the incubation time of a single test, which is longer and overlaps with other tests.

problem: A reagent blank does not correct reagent carryover. A blank corrects the absorbance of the reagent itself; carryover is corrected by adequate washing and by carryover studies with a high-reagent sample followed by a blank.
fix: Forgetting reagent carryover: a trace of the previous reagent raises the next result slightly, so an effective wash step is needed and carryover must be checked by running a blank after a high-reagent sample, not by a reagent blank.

problem: 'Enzyme tests are read as a rate and never as a final absorbance' is too absolute; some enzyme methods are fixed-time or end-point colorimetric assays that are read once after a set incubation.
fix: Enzyme tests are usually read as a rate, because activity is proportional to ΔA/min; some fixed-time methods read one absorbance after a set incubation, but a true rate method cannot be read as an end point.
